stem: A startup's generative AI app has unpredictable traffic: some days see a few hundred requests, others see bursts of thousands. The team wants to pay only for what it uses.
prompt: Which Amazon Bedrock pricing option fits BEST?

options.text: On-demand pricing, billed per input and output token
options.why: On-demand charges only for tokens processed, with no commitment, which suits unpredictable or variable traffic.

options.text: Provisioned Throughput with a six-month commitment
options.why: Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity billed by the hour regardless of use, which wastes money when traffic is low and unpredictable.

options.text: Reserved Instances for Amazon RDS
options.why: RDS Reserved Instances discount database instances and have nothing to do with Bedrock model inference.

options.text: Buying dedicated GPU servers on premises
options.why: On-premises hardware requires large upfront cost and capacity planning, the opposite of paying per use.

explanation.answer: Amazon Bedrock on-demand pricing charges per input and output token (or per image for image models) with no commitments. It is the most flexible option for variable or early-stage workloads.
explanation.concept: Provisioned Throughput buys dedicated model capacity (model units) by the hour, optionally with term commitments, giving guaranteed throughput for steady, high-volume workloads.
explanation.examTip: Unpredictable traffic, pay per use = on-demand. Steady high volume needing guaranteed capacity = Provisioned Throughput.

references.title: Increase model invocation capacity with Provisioned Throughput

stem: A large retailer's product-search assistant handles a steady, very high volume of requests all day. It has experienced throttling during peaks and needs consistent, guaranteed throughput.
prompt: Which Amazon Bedrock option addresses this?

options.text: Lowering the temperature
options.why: Temperature affects output randomness, not capacity or throttling.

options.text: Provisioned Throughput
options.why: Provisioned Throughput reserves dedicated capacity for a model, giving consistent throughput for steady, high-volume workloads.

options.text: Using a larger embedding dimension
options.why: Embedding dimension affects retrieval, not model throughput.

options.text: Batch inference
options.why: Batch inference processes requests asynchronously at lower cost. It does not suit an interactive assistant that needs immediate responses.

explanation.answer: Provisioned Throughput lets you purchase model units that deliver a dedicated level of throughput for a model, billed hourly, with optional 1-month or 6-month commitments for lower rates. It suits predictable, high-volume production workloads that need guaranteed capacity.
explanation.concept: Cross-Region inference is another way to handle bursts with on-demand models by routing requests across Regions.
explanation.examTip: Steady high volume + guaranteed throughput = Provisioned Throughput.

references.title: Increase model invocation capacity with Provisioned Throughput

stem: A media company needs to generate summaries for 2 million archived articles. Results are needed within a few days, not in real time, and cost is the top priority.
prompt: Which Amazon Bedrock approach is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: Purchase Provisioned Throughput for a year
options.why: A long commitment for a one-time job is wasteful. Batch inference is designed for this pattern.

options.text: Use the Bedrock console playground manually
options.why: Manually running millions of prompts is impractical.

options.text: Batch inference, submitting the prompts as a job from Amazon S3
options.why: Bedrock batch inference processes large sets of prompts asynchronously at a lower price than on-demand for supported models.

options.text: Send 2 million real-time on-demand requests as fast as possible
options.why: Real-time on-demand requests cost more per token than batch processing and risk throttling, with no benefit when results can wait.

explanation.answer: Amazon Bedrock batch inference runs many prompts asynchronously: you place input records in Amazon S3, start a job, and receive outputs in S3. For supported models it is priced lower than on-demand inference, making it ideal for large, non-urgent workloads.
explanation.concept: Trade-off: batch is cheaper but not immediate. Choose it when latency does not matter.
explanation.examTip: Huge volume, not time-sensitive, cost matters = Bedrock batch inference.

references.title: Process multiple prompts with batch inference

stem: An application using an on-demand model in one AWS Region sometimes hits throughput limits during traffic spikes. The team wants higher throughput and resilience without managing capacity.
prompt: Which Amazon Bedrock feature helps?

options.text: Provisioned Throughput for the model in that Region
options.why: Provisioned Throughput adds dedicated capacity, but the team would have to size and manage it, which it wants to avoid.

options.text: Batch inference for requests that arrive during spikes
options.why: Batch inference is asynchronous, so users would not get real-time responses during spikes.

options.text: Prompt caching for the application's repeated prompts
options.why: Caching reduces cost and latency per request but does not raise the Region's throughput limits.

options.text: Cross-Region inference using an inference profile
options.why: Cross-Region inference routes on-demand requests to Regions with capacity, increasing throughput and resilience without managing capacity.

explanation.answer: Cross-Region inference uses inference profiles to route on-demand requests to Regions with available capacity within a defined geography. It improves throughput and availability during spikes without requiring Provisioned Throughput.
explanation.concept: Consider data residency requirements: choose inference profiles whose Regions are acceptable for your compliance needs.
explanation.examTip: On-demand throttling during bursts, no capacity management = cross-Region inference.

stem: A company's monthly Amazon Bedrock bill is dominated by a large premium model that classifies customer FAQs into 12 categories. The prompts are short, traffic varies widely through the day, and users need an answer in real time. A test shows that a smaller model in the same family classifies the FAQs with the same accuracy.
prompt: Which change will reduce cost the MOST while still meeting these requirements?

options.text: Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the premium model
options.why: Provisioned Throughput is billed by the hour for dedicated capacity. With widely varying traffic much of it would sit idle, and the company would still be paying premium-model rates for a task a smaller model handles.

options.text: Send the FAQ requests to Bedrock batch inference
options.why: Batch inference is cheaper per token, but it processes requests asynchronously. Users need answers in real time, so batch does not meet the requirements.

options.text: Enable prompt caching for the FAQ classification prompts
options.why: Prompt caching saves money when a long, identical prefix is reused. These prompts are short, so there is little to cache and the premium per-token price still applies.

options.text: Switch the FAQ classification to the smaller model
options.why: The smaller model meets the accuracy requirement at a much lower per-token price, works on demand for variable traffic, and answers in real time.

explanation.answer: When a cheaper model meets the quality bar, right-sizing the model is usually the biggest saving, because per-token prices differ widely between models. It also keeps on-demand pricing, which fits variable traffic, and real-time responses.
explanation.concept: Match each Bedrock cost lever to its workload: smaller models for simple tasks; batch inference for non-urgent bulk work; prompt caching for long repeated prefixes; Provisioned Throughput for steady, high, predictable traffic.
explanation.examTip: Check the constraints before choosing a cost lever: "real time" rules out batch, "short prompts" weakens prompt caching, and "variable traffic" argues against Provisioned Throughput.

references.title: Process multiple prompts with batch inference

stem: A company is deciding whether to fine-tune a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock or improve results with prompt engineering and RAG.
prompt: Which cost consideration about fine-tuned (custom) models is MOST accurate?

options.text: Custom models run at no charge once training finishes
options.why: Inference on custom models is billed, and model storage or dedicated capacity often adds cost.

options.text: They add training cost plus ongoing storage and serving costs
options.why: Fine-tuning incurs training charges, and custom models bring storage and serving costs, so they usually cost more than prompts and RAG.

options.text: They cost the same to run as the base model, with no extras
options.why: Custom models are separate resources with their own deployment options and storage charges.

options.text: Prompting needs GPU training time, so it costs more than tuning
options.why: Prompt engineering involves no training at all; it is the cheapest customization approach.

explanation.answer: Fine-tuning adds training cost, and custom models bring ongoing costs such as model storage and, depending on the model, dedicated capacity like Provisioned Throughput for inference. Prompt engineering and RAG usually achieve the goal at lower cost and should be tried first.
explanation.concept: Customization approaches from lowest to highest cost: prompt engineering, RAG, fine-tuning, continued pre-training, pre-training from scratch.
explanation.examTip: Custom models = training cost + ongoing hosting/storage cost. Try prompts and RAG first.

stem: A company planning to launch in a new country discovers that the specific foundation model it wants is not available in the AWS Region closest to its users.
prompt: Which trade-off must the company consider?

options.text: Wait for the model to arrive in the closest Region
options.why: Waiting delays the launch indefinitely; the company needs to choose among workable options now.

options.text: Data residency rules do not apply to model inference
options.why: Prompts can contain personal data, so residency and privacy rules apply to inference too.

options.text: Choose another model, another Region or cross-Region inference
options.why: Model availability varies by Region, so the company must weigh alternatives against latency and data residency.

options.text: Reach the model through a VPC endpoint in the closest Region
options.why: A VPC endpoint provides private connectivity to services in that Region; it cannot make an unavailable model available.

explanation.answer: Regional coverage is one of the cost and design trade-offs for AWS generative AI services. Model availability differs by Region, and choosing a Region affects latency, data residency compliance, pricing and redundancy options.
explanation.concept: Cross-Region inference can expand capacity, but teams must confirm that routing across the included Regions satisfies their compliance requirements.
explanation.examTip: Model not in your Region → weigh another model, another Region or cross-Region inference against latency and residency.

stem: A legal assistant sends the same 40-page contract as context with each of many follow-up questions in a session. Costs and latency are high because the contract tokens are processed every time.
prompt: Which Amazon Bedrock feature directly reduces cost and latency for this pattern?

options.text: Increasing the temperature
options.why: Temperature affects randomness and does not reduce processing of repeated tokens.

options.text: Adding more examples to the prompt
options.why: More examples add tokens and increase cost.

options.text: Switching to a diffusion model
options.why: Diffusion models generate images and cannot answer contract questions.

options.text: Prompt caching for the repeated prompt prefix
options.why: Prompt caching stores the processed repeated portion of a prompt, so subsequent requests reuse it at lower cost and with lower latency.

explanation.answer: Prompt caching lets supported models cache a repeated prompt prefix, such as a long document or system instructions, across requests. Cached tokens are billed at a reduced rate and processed faster, lowering both cost and latency for workloads that reuse context.
explanation.concept: Prompt caching is listed in the exam guide as an FM selection and cost consideration. Structure prompts so stable content comes first and changing questions come last.
explanation.examTip: Same long context reused across requests = prompt caching.

references.title: Prompt caching for faster model inference

stem: A company's mission-critical customer assistant must stay responsive during traffic spikes and remain available during a Regional disruption. A cheaper design uses a single Region with on-demand capacity only.
prompt: Which statement BEST describes the trade-off?

options.text: Reserved capacity and multi-Region redundancy cost more
options.why: Guaranteed capacity and redundancy add cost, which the business weighs against the impact of slowdowns or outages.

options.text: Multi-Region costs the same, since only tokens are billed
options.why: Running the application across Regions adds infrastructure and operational costs beyond tokens.

options.text: On-demand capacity alone keeps it responsive during spikes
options.why: On-demand requests can be throttled during spikes; keeping responsiveness under load needs extra capacity, which costs more.

options.text: Redundancy lowers total cost by spreading traffic
options.why: Running in more places or reserving capacity typically increases cost.

explanation.answer: Cost trade-offs for AWS generative AI services include responsiveness (latency and capacity), availability, redundancy, performance, regional coverage, token-based pricing, provisioned throughput and custom models. More resilience and guaranteed performance usually cost more.
explanation.concept: Match the design to the business impact: mission-critical workloads justify reserved capacity and redundancy, while internal tools may accept the cheaper option.
explanation.examTip: Better availability and guaranteed speed cost more. Decide by business criticality.

references.title: Increase model invocation capacity with Provisioned Throughput

stem: An analyst estimates monthly costs for an on-demand text model. The application sends about 2,000 input tokens and receives about 500 output tokens per request.
prompt: Which statement about the cost calculation is correct?

options.text: Cost depends on requests, since each has a fixed price
options.why: Token-based pricing means longer requests and responses cost more; there is no fixed price per request.

options.text: Input and output tokens are both billed, at different rates
options.why: Pricing is per input token and per output token, usually at different rates, so both volumes must be modeled.

options.text: Only output tokens are billed; input tokens are free
options.why: On-demand text models bill for input tokens too, which matters here with 2,000 per request.

options.text: Input and output tokens are billed at one flat rate
options.why: Output tokens are typically priced higher than input tokens, so a single rate would misestimate cost.

explanation.answer: On-demand pricing for text models is based on input tokens processed and output tokens generated, typically with separate rates. Estimating cost requires request volume × (input tokens × input rate + output tokens × output rate).
explanation.concept: Reducing either side helps: shorter prompts and retrieved context reduce input tokens; concise answers and max-token limits reduce output tokens.
explanation.examTip: Cost = requests × (input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price).

stem: A company gets excellent results from a large, expensive model on a narrow, repetitive task, but the inference cost is too high at its volume. It wants a smaller model that performs nearly as well on this specific task.
prompt: Which Amazon Bedrock capability is designed for this?

options.text: Guardrails
options.why: Guardrails filter content and do not create a smaller model.

options.text: Increasing the context window
options.why: A bigger context window does not make the model cheaper.

options.text: Model distillation
options.why: Distillation uses a large teacher model's responses to train a smaller student model that approaches the teacher's quality on the target task at lower cost and latency.

options.text: Model invocation logging
options.why: Logging records requests and responses. It does not reduce model cost by itself.

explanation.answer: Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation transfers knowledge from a larger teacher model to a smaller student model for a specific use case. The distilled model can be faster and cheaper while retaining much of the teacher's accuracy on that task.
explanation.concept: Distillation is one of the customization approaches in the exam guide, alongside pre-training, fine-tuning, in-context learning and RAG, each with different cost trade-offs.
explanation.examTip: Large model quality, smaller model cost, specific task = distillation.

references.title: Customize a model with distillation in Amazon Bedrock

stem: A company debates self-hosting an open-weight model on GPU instances versus using a managed on-demand API. Its traffic is low and irregular, and it has no ML infrastructure engineers.
prompt: Which option is MOST likely to have the lower total cost of ownership?

options.text: Training a new model from scratch
options.why: Pre-training from scratch is extremely expensive and does not reduce operating cost.

options.text: Buying on-premises GPU servers
options.why: Upfront hardware cost and maintenance far exceed the needs of a low-traffic workload.

options.text: Self-hosting on GPU instances that run 24/7
options.why: Always-on GPUs bill continuously even when idle, and the company would need engineers to operate them.

options.text: The managed on-demand API, paying per token
options.why: With low, irregular traffic and no infrastructure team, paying only for tokens used avoids idle GPU cost and operational overhead.

explanation.answer: Total cost of ownership includes infrastructure, idle capacity, operations staff and maintenance. Managed per-token APIs are usually cheapest for low or variable traffic. Self-hosting can win at sustained high utilization with in-house expertise.
explanation.concept: Consider utilization: idle dedicated capacity is wasted money, while per-token pricing scales to zero.
explanation.examTip: Low/irregular traffic + no infra team = managed per-token API.

stem: A team wants to reduce inference costs for its Amazon Bedrock application without degrading quality.
prompt: Which actions reduce cost? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Raise max tokens so long responses are not truncated
options.why: Allowing longer responses increases output tokens and cost.

options.text: Use the largest model for all requests to reduce retries
options.why: Larger models cost more per token, which outweighs any savings from fewer retries on simple tasks.

options.text: Buy Provisioned Throughput for low, irregular traffic
options.why: Dedicated capacity is billed hourly, so with low, irregular traffic most of it sits idle and costs more.

options.text: Use batch inference for nightly, non-urgent report generation
options.why: Batch inference is priced lower than on-demand for supported models when results can wait.

options.text: Retrieve only the most relevant document chunks instead of entire documents
options.why: Sending fewer, more relevant tokens reduces input token cost and often improves answer focus.

explanation.answer: Common cost optimizations for generative AI include reducing input tokens (concise prompts, targeted retrieval, summarized history), limiting output length, choosing smaller models where adequate, using batch inference for non-urgent work, prompt caching for repeated context, and the right capacity model.
explanation.concept: Measure quality with evaluation datasets after each optimization so savings do not come at the cost of accuracy.
explanation.examTip: Fewer tokens, right-sized models, batch for non-urgent work, caching for repeated context.

references.title: Process multiple prompts with batch inference

stem: A marketing team budgets for an image-generation model on Amazon Bedrock.
prompt: How are image-generation models typically priced on-demand?

options.text: Per image generated, varying by size and quality
options.why: Image models are commonly priced per generated image, with the price depending on resolution and quality.

options.text: Per input token of the text prompt only
options.why: Text tokens are the unit for text models; image generation is priced by the images produced.

options.text: Per hour that the model is deployed
options.why: Hourly billing applies to dedicated capacity such as Provisioned Throughput, not on-demand use.

options.text: A flat monthly fee for unlimited images
options.why: On-demand pricing is usage-based, not unlimited.

explanation.answer: Pricing depends on modality: text models are usually priced per input and output token, while image-generation models are typically priced per image, varying with resolution and quality. Video generation is typically priced by output duration.
explanation.concept: Check each model's pricing details because units differ by modality and provider.
explanation.examTip: Text = per token. Images = per image (by size/quality).

stem: A voice assistant must begin speaking a reply within about half a second. The current large model is accurate but takes several seconds to start responding.
prompt: Which change MOST directly improves responsiveness?

options.text: Switch to Provisioned Throughput for the large model
options.why: Dedicated capacity prevents throttling but does not make the large model start responding faster.

options.text: Use a smaller or latency-optimized model and stream the reply
options.why: Smaller or latency-optimized models produce first tokens sooner, and streaming lets speech start as soon as they arrive.

options.text: Add prompt caching for the system prompt
options.why: Caching can trim some processing time, but it cannot close a gap of several seconds on a large model.

options.text: Raise max tokens so each reply completes in one call
options.why: Allowing longer replies does not make the first tokens arrive sooner.

explanation.answer: Latency depends on model size, input length, output length and serving configuration. For interactive experiences, smaller or latency-optimized models, shorter prompts and streaming responses improve perceived responsiveness.
explanation.concept: Performance trade-offs often pit accuracy against speed and cost. Evaluate whether a smaller model meets quality needs.
explanation.examTip: Too slow to respond → smaller/faster model + streaming + shorter prompts.

stem: A nonprofit wants to pilot a generative AI chatbot for three months with uncertain usage and a small budget.
prompt: Which characteristic of AWS generative AI services MOST helps?

options.text: Mandatory multi-year contracts
options.why: AWS generative AI services do not require multi-year contracts for on-demand use.

options.text: Required purchase of on-premises hardware
options.why: Managed services run in the cloud. No hardware purchase is needed.

options.text: Pay-as-you-go pricing with no upfront commitment
options.why: Paying only for actual usage keeps pilot costs proportional to traffic and avoids long-term commitments.

options.text: Fixed pricing regardless of usage
options.why: On-demand pricing scales with usage rather than being fixed.

explanation.answer: AWS generative AI services such as Amazon Bedrock offer pay-as-you-go pricing, which makes experimentation and pilots cost-effective because spending tracks actual usage.
explanation.concept: Set budgets and alerts with AWS Budgets and monitor token usage to avoid surprises during pilots.
explanation.examTip: Uncertain usage + small budget = pay as you go.

stem: A team can either paste an entire 500-page manual into a long-context model on every question, or retrieve the five most relevant passages with RAG.
prompt: Which statement about the cost trade-off is MOST accurate?

options.text: Pasting the manual is cheaper because there is no vector store
options.why: Hundreds of thousands of tokens per question cost far more than a vector store at most volumes.

options.text: Both cost the same, since the model reads the same facts
options.why: Token volumes differ by orders of magnitude, so costs differ significantly.

options.text: RAG costs more, because embeddings cost as much as output tokens
options.why: Embedding is done once per chunk at ingestion and is cheap compared with sending a whole manual on every question.

options.text: RAG sends far fewer input tokens, though it adds retrieval costs
options.why: Sending a few relevant passages instead of the whole manual cuts input tokens dramatically, outweighing retrieval costs.

explanation.answer: Because generative models charge per token, sending only relevant context through RAG is usually much cheaper and faster than sending entire documents on every request. RAG does add costs for embeddings, vector storage and retrieval, which are generally small by comparison at scale.
explanation.concept: Long-context approaches can still be useful for tasks that truly need the whole document at once, and prompt caching can reduce their cost for repeated use.
explanation.examTip: Whole document every time = many tokens. RAG = few relevant tokens.

stem: A company is confident its high-volume workload will run steadily for at least the next six months and wants the lowest hourly rate for dedicated Bedrock model capacity.
prompt: Which option provides this?

options.text: Provisioned Throughput with a six-month commitment
options.why: A longer commitment term lowers the hourly rate for dedicated capacity, rewarding predictable long-term usage.

options.text: Provisioned Throughput with no commitment
options.why: No-commitment provisioned capacity is more flexible but costs more per hour than a committed term.

options.text: On-demand pricing with cross-Region inference
options.why: On-demand does not provide dedicated capacity or an hourly commitment discount.

options.text: Batch inference scheduled throughout the day
options.why: Batch is asynchronous and does not provide dedicated capacity for a steady interactive workload.

explanation.answer: Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput is purchased in model units billed hourly. Choosing a commitment term (such as 1 month or 6 months) lowers the effective rate compared with no-commitment provisioned capacity, rewarding predictable long-term usage.
explanation.concept: Commitments trade flexibility for lower prices. Use them only when demand is predictable.
explanation.examTip: Predictable long-term volume → commit to get a lower rate.

references.title: Increase model invocation capacity with Provisioned Throughput

stem: A team deploys a chatbot on Amazon Bedrock and assumes AWS is responsible for everything about it, including what users are allowed to ask and who can access the application.
prompt: Under the AWS shared responsibility model, which is the customer's responsibility?

options.text: Securing the physical data centers that run Bedrock
options.why: Physical security of facilities is AWS's responsibility.

options.text: IAM access, data protection, guardrails and use of outputs
options.why: Customers are responsible for security in the cloud: identities, data, application behavior and responsible use of outputs.

options.text: Patching and operating the Bedrock service itself
options.why: AWS operates and patches the managed Bedrock service.

options.text: Isolating its prompts from other Bedrock customers
options.why: Isolation between customers in the managed service is AWS's responsibility.

explanation.answer: AWS is responsible for security of the cloud (infrastructure, hardware, managed service operation). Customers are responsible for security in the cloud: IAM permissions, data classification and encryption choices, network configuration, guardrails, prompt and output handling, and compliance of their application.
explanation.concept: With managed services, the customer's share shrinks but never disappears. Responsible AI decisions remain with the customer.
explanation.examTip: AWS = of the cloud. Customer = in the cloud (data, access, configuration, use).

stem: A team's agent costs far more per task than a simple chatbot. Traces show the agent makes many model calls per task, each carrying long tool descriptions and growing history.
prompt: Which statement BEST explains the cost and a mitigation?

options.text: Agents are billed per task, so the fix is running fewer tasks
options.why: Model usage is billed by tokens, not per task; the design can be changed to use fewer tokens per task.

options.text: Tool calls are billed like output tokens, so remove the tools
options.why: Removing tools would break the agent; cost comes from model calls carrying large context.

options.text: Each step is a model call with context; cut steps, context and model size
options.why: Agent cost scales with steps times tokens, so limiting steps, trimming context and using smaller models for simple steps reduces it.

options.text: Agents use larger models by default; switch to batch inference
options.why: Batch inference is asynchronous and unsuitable for interactive agents, and agents do not default to larger models.

explanation.answer: Agentic applications typically invoke the model several times per task (planning, tool selection, reflection, final answer), and each call includes instructions, tool definitions and history. Costs scale with steps × tokens. Mitigations include step limits, concise tool descriptions, context summarization, prompt caching and routing simple steps to smaller models.
explanation.concept: Track cost per task (cost per interaction) as a business metric alongside task completion rate.
explanation.examTip: Agent cost ≈ number of steps × tokens per step. Reduce both.

references.title: Prompt caching for faster model inference
